title: When the Light Can't Get Through

patient.name: Mr Rajendran s/o Muthu
patient.presenting_complaint: Here for biometry before cataract surgery; the optical (light) biometer could not get a reading because the cataract is very dense

history.hpc: Mr Rajendran is booked for left eye cataract surgery. Optical biometry failed to capture the axial length because the cataract is very dense and blocks the light. He asks: 'My cataract very thick already, the machine just now cannot read is it?' The OT must switch to A-scan ultrasound biometry to obtain the axial length.
history.pmhx: Dense mature cataract left eye. Type 2 diabetes, hypertension.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Left eye: dense (mature) cataract blocking optical biometry; right eye moderate lens changes
examination_findings.fundus: Left fundus not visible due to dense cataract

investigations.ascan_biometry: A-scan ultrasound biometry performed for the left eye to obtain axial length when optical biometry failed. Using the contact (applanation) technique, a topical anaesthetic was instilled first; care taken to avoid corneal indentation (which falsely shortens axial length). Immersion technique is an alternative that avoids indentation. Multiple consistent axial length readings obtained and documented; keratometry obtained separately.
investigations.measurement_quality: Several consistent A-scan readings; minimal corneal compression; values within a plausible range.

diagnosis: A-scan ultrasound biometry used to measure axial length for IOL calculation when optical biometry failed due to a dense cataract. The OT competency is choosing A-scan appropriately, preparing the patient (topical anaesthetic for contact method), avoiding corneal indentation error, and documenting reliable measurements.

immediate: Recognise that a dense cataract blocking optical biometry is an indication for A-scan ultrasound
Explain the procedure; for the contact method, instil topical anaesthetic and confirm no allergy
Use correct technique to avoid corneal indentation (or use the immersion method), which can falsely shorten the axial length
Take multiple readings and check they are consistent before accepting
Document diagnosis, indication, RE/LE, preparation (anaesthetic), and axial length findings
Obtain keratometry separately and hand measurements to the doctor for IOL calculation
follow_up: Doctor to calculate IOL power using the A-scan axial length and keratometry
Document the reason optical biometry was not used
patient_education: Explain that because the cataract is very dense, an ultrasound (touch) method is needed instead of the light scan
Explain the numbing drop and that the probe gently touches the eye briefly
Reassure him it is quick and that the measurements help choose the lens
Advise not to rub the eye until the anaesthetic wears off

key_points: Confirms the indication (cataract surgery) and the operative eye
Recognises why optical biometry failed (dense cataract)
Checks for anaesthetic drop allergy before the contact method
Explains the A-scan procedure to the patient
Selects A-scan ultrasound appropriately when optical biometry fails
Prepares correctly (topical anaesthetic for contact technique)
Avoids corneal indentation error or uses the immersion method
Takes multiple consistent readings and documents axial length
Understands a dense cataract is an indication for A-scan biometry
Knows corneal indentation falsely shortens axial length
Recognises the measurements are for IOL power calculation
Knows IOL selection is the doctor's role
Obtains reliable axial length and keratometry and documents them
Documents the reason optical biometry was not used and the preparation
Explains the contact ultrasound method and aftercare to the patient
Hands measurements to the doctor for IOL calculation
